title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 40 — Securities to be dealt with in stock exchanges

content.overview: Section 40 governs a company making a public offer by requiring an application to one or more recognised stock exchanges and permission for the securities to be dealt with there before the public offer. It also ring-fences public application monies in a separate scheduled-bank account and restricts their use.
content.glance: Section 40 — Securities to be dealt with in stock exchanges
content.study:
Section 40 governs a company making a public offer by requiring an application to one or more recognised stock exchanges and permission for the securities to be dealt with there before the public offer. It also ring-fences public application monies in a separate scheduled-bank account and restricts their use.

Statutory test
1. Public offer: the company is making a public offer of securities.
2. Stock-exchange application and permission: before the public offer, the company must apply to one or more recognised stock exchanges and obtain permission for the securities to be dealt with there.
3. Prospectus disclosure: where the prospectus states that such an application has been made, it must state the name or names of the stock exchange(s) in which the securities will be dealt with.
4. Separate bank account: all public application monies for subscription must be kept in a separate account with a scheduled bank.
5. Permitted use only: those monies may be used only for adjustment against allotment where the securities are permitted to be dealt with on the exchange(s) named in the prospectus, or for repayment within the SEBI-specified time where the company cannot allot securities for another reason.
6. No waiver: a condition attempting to make an applicant waive compliance with section 40 is void.
7. Default consequence: contravention attracts the statutory company/officer consequences in the section, subject to the current text and amendments.
8. Commission: the section permits payment of commission in connection with subscription subject to prescribed conditions.

Application
A company collects ₹50 crore from public applicants, places it in its ordinary operating account and uses ₹5 crore for unrelated expenses while exchange permission remains unresolved. Identify the section 40 defects, distinguish the exchange-permission issue from the money-use issue, and state the statutory consequence without importing a remedy not supported by the section.

Boundary
Section 40 is distinct from section 39: section 39 focuses on minimum subscription, application money and return of allotment; section 40 focuses on exchange permission and protection of public application monies. Section 29 addresses dematerialised form for public offers, while section 40 addresses exchange dealing and money handling.

sections.heading: Detailed legal explanation
sections.body: Section 40 must be read with the public-offer regime rather than as a general listing rule for every company transaction. Its first limb concerns exchange permission before the public offer. Its second limb protects application money by requiring segregation and limiting use. The prospectus statement about the exchange must correspond to the statutory requirement. A contractual or application-form term cannot cure non-compliance by forcing investors to waive section 40.

sections.heading: Practical illustrations
sections.body:
A company proposes a public offer but has not obtained the required recognised-stock-exchange permission. The public offer cannot simply proceed on the theory that permission can be obtained later.

Application money is collected into a general operating account and spent on unrelated expenses. That use conflicts with the statutory segregation/use restriction.

An application form says the subscriber waives section 40 compliance. The waiver condition is void.

cases.name: Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd.
cases.facts: A properly incorporated company was challenged as indistinct from its controlling shareholder.
cases.issue: What is the legal effect of incorporation?
cases.ratioDecidendi: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members, even when control and ownership are concentrated.
cases.holding: The company's separate personality was affirmed.
cases.relevance: Use for Companies Act s. 9 and corporate personality.

cases.name: Foss v. Harbottle
cases.facts: Shareholders sought relief for alleged wrongs to the company.
cases.issue: Who may sue for a wrong done to the company and when may exceptions apply?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The company is the proper plaintiff for corporate wrongs, subject to recognised exceptions such as fraud on the minority and ultra vires acts.
cases.holding: The proper-plaintiff and majority-rule principles were established.
cases.relevance: Use with oppression, mismanagement and class-action analysis.

cases.name: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined share issue powers and alleged oppression.
cases.issue: When does a corporate action become oppressive or invalid?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examines purpose, fairness, statutory power and resulting prejudice rather than treating every irregularity as oppression.
cases.holding: The corporate action was assessed under the statutory and equitable framework.
cases.relevance: Use for share allotment and oppression claims.

cases.name: Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court reviewed a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the company court.
cases.issue: What is the court's role in sanctioning a corporate scheme?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The court must ensure statutory compliance, class fairness, informed approval and absence of illegality, but does not substitute its commercial judgment for the company's decision.
cases.holding: The principles governing scheme sanction were stated.
cases.relevance: Use for corporate arrangements and tribunal scrutiny.
